listen: Good morning. This is The Daily Brief for Sunday, November 22. Our lead story is about Anthropic. NPR reports that a mathematician who works for the company claims he has solved a Holy Grail of math problems with help from Claude. This is his claim, and the report does not say whether others have checked it. NPR notes it is the second time in recent months that an AI company, or someone linked to one, has made such a claim about a famed unsolved problem. Now the front page. In the UFC, Navajo Stirling knocked out former champion Jirí Procházka in the second round of the main event in Doha, Qatar. He is now seven and zero in the UFC. In the NBA, Rockets coach Ime Udoka was upset after the loss to the Nuggets. Houston gave up a season high in points, and he called the defense as bad as he has seen it. In politics, President Trump is directing federal contractors to consult the White House about inquiries from Congress. They are also told to withhold any communications that his administration considers privileged. In Atlanta, Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger certified Georgia's November third election results on Friday. That makes the Democratic sweep of statewide offices official. Now the sections. In tech, a Claude Code skill bundle for bug hunting is trending on GitHub, and Graham Dumpleton has released Muru, an AI-assisted Rust server for Python web apps. In politics, The Lever compares Chris Van Hollen and Chuck Schumer on key issues, and Drop Site News reports that Sudan's power grid is near collapse after strikes on electricity stations. In world news, South Korea's education minister resigned over chaos linked to measures against AI-assisted cheating on the college entrance exam. Mexican authorities captured a cartel leader on the FBI's most wanted list, in a firefight that left eleven dead. Bayer reached a Roundup settlement that could cost the company billions. In sports, the Forty-Niners play in Mexico City tonight, and Fred Warner is building a strong Defensive Player of the Year case. The Rockets are also getting a boost from a healthy Fred VanVleet. In Atlanta, Fulton County commissioners clashed over security for incoming chair Mo Ivory, and MARTA installed its final upgraded faregate. In architecture, a London steel reuse project used Tekla automation, and the Paris Aquatics Centre shows a curved wooden form. In science, Science News reports that the world is bracing for a strong El Niño, and NASA shared drifting twilight clouds seen by the Curiosity rover on Mars. That is the brief. Have a good day. This is the Sunday edition. Here is the week in review. Anthropic goes public as markets slide; Trump meets Xi, Putin. Anthropic was the main story this week. On Monday it filed an S-1 with the SEC, launched its roadshow and put a portion of its shares into a new Public Benefit Fund. NPR reported that the IPO priced at $83 a share and raised a record $81.3 billion. Anthropic announced the closing on Saturday. It also expanded its partnership with the GSA, and the Claude Platform added Linked billing in beta. Mathematician Levent Alpöge says he and Claude found a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis. NPR reports this as his claim. Markets fell late in the week: the S&P 500 dropped 3.7% on Friday, and the Nasdaq is now down for the year. In world news, President Trump met Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin. NPR Politics reported few concrete results beyond a joint statement on some issues. Ukraine struck the Crimean Bridge, and a Russian missile attack hit three Kyiv bridges and killed five people. Iran stepped up attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz and on several Gulf countries. The UN's top court ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya. COP31 talks stalled over fossil fuels. In the US, NPR reported that Democrats won 56% of the House vote to Republicans' 42%. Mary Peltola won Alaska's Senate seat, and Brad Raffensperger certified Georgia's results. lead.title: Anthropic worker claims to have solved a Holy Grail of math problems with the help of AI
lead.note: NPR reports that a mathematician who works for Anthropic claims he has solved what it calls a Holy Grail of math problems, using the company's AI tool Claude. The summary presents this as his claim, and it does not say whether other mathematicians have checked the work. NPR also notes that this is the second time in recent months that an AI company, or someone linked to one, has claimed to have cracked a famed unsolved math problem. For a reader who builds personal tools with Claude, the story shows the kind of hard technical work people are now trying with these systems. It is worth reading as a claim for now. The real test will be whether outside experts review the result and agree that it holds up, which the short summary does not yet describe.

week.headline: Anthropic goes public as markets slide; Trump meets Xi, Putin
week.summary:
Anthropic was the main story this week. On Monday it filed an S-1 with the SEC, launched its roadshow and put a portion of its shares into a new Public Benefit Fund. NPR reported that the IPO priced at $83 a share and raised a record $81.3 billion. Anthropic announced the closing on Saturday. It also expanded its partnership with the GSA, and the Claude Platform added Linked billing in beta. Mathematician Levent Alpöge says he and Claude found a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis. NPR reports this as his claim. Markets fell late in the week: the S&P 500 dropped 3.7% on Friday, and the Nasdaq is now down for the year.

In world news, President Trump met Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin. NPR Politics reported few concrete results beyond a joint statement on some issues. Ukraine struck the Crimean Bridge, and a Russian missile attack hit three Kyiv bridges and killed five people. Iran stepped up attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz and on several Gulf countries. The UN's top court ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya. COP31 talks stalled over fossil fuels. In the US, NPR reported that Democrats won 56% of the House vote to Republicans' 42%. Mary Peltola won Alaska's Senate seat, and Brad Raffensperger certified Georgia's results.

In Atlanta, a $19B regional plan includes millions for The Stitch, and Underground Atlanta's owner bought a John Portman tower. In BIM, Pliera launched as a challenger to Revit. The 49ers beat Dallas 46-40. The Rockets reached 12-4 before losing to Denver.
